html:
The Kiowa, who call themselves Gáuigú, are a Plains people now based in southwestern Oklahoma. This map territory shows their later homeland on the southern Plains; in 1492 their ancestors probably lived far to the north, near the upper Missouri.

They speak a Kiowa-Tanoan language. After horses reached the Plains they moved south and became mounted bison hunters. Around 1790 they made a lasting peace with the Comanche, and the two raided together deep into Texas and Mexico. Kiowa artists kept painted calendars that recorded each summer and winter.

The Medicine Lodge Treaty of 1867 confined them to a reservation in Indian Territory. The writer N. Scott Momaday, who won the Pulitzer Prize in 1969, was Kiowa. See also Kiowa and Kiowa, Comanche and Apache land in Oklahoma.
